draft.title: Judging science in the media
card: Media includes news, websites, videos and social media. Some science claims in the media are sound and some are not.
A claim is more trustworthy when it names its source, so you can check where it came from.
It is also more trustworthy when it shows its evidence, such as data from a test, and when it comes from experts in that field.
Be careful with claims based on opinion, or from someone selling a product. They may leave out evidence that does not help the sale.
draft.remember: Trust claims that name a source, show evidence and come from experts, not opinion or sales.

a.q: Which claim is the most trustworthy?
opts: A university team reports test results and names the journal
A famous singer says a tea cures colds, from her own use
An advert says nine in ten love a cream, with no source
A post says a diet works because a friend lost weight
a.why: The first claim names a source, shows results and comes from experts. The advert sounds like evidence, but it has no named source and it is selling something.
a.clue: Look for a named source and evidence from experts.

b.q: A video claims a new drink makes you smarter. The video is made by the company that sells the drink. What is the best response?
opts: Look for evidence from independent experts first
Believe it, because videos show real products
Believe it, because the drink company knows its product
Ignore it because all science claims are false
b.why: The company is selling something, so the claim needs checking against independent experts and evidence. Not all science claims are false, so rejecting every claim is also wrong.
b.clue: Who gains if you buy the drink?

a.best: A university team reports test results and names the journal

b.best: Look for evidence from independent experts first

problems.detail: Why (a) says 'The first claim names a source', but options appear in random order, and the university claim is not first as shown. Students would read this as praising the singer's claim. Refer to the claim by its content, not its position.

The remember line says 'Trust claims that name a source…', which is more absolute than the card's 'more trustworthy'. It suggests such claims can simply be trusted, rather than judged more trustworthy.

The right option relies on 'independent experts', a term the card never introduces. The card only speaks of experts in the field and of claims from sellers, so students must infer what 'independent' means.
The right option stands out: the other three are 'Believe it…' twice and an extreme 'all science claims are false'. A student can pick it by elimination without knowing the idea.
